chunks: "It matters because digital inputs react to threshold crossings, and a non-monotonic edge crosses the threshold more than once.
On a clock or any edge-triggered input, that's extra edges: a counter counts twice, a flip-flop captures at the wrong time, a state machine advances when it shouldn't.
On reset or interrupt pins it can cause spurious resets or interrupts.
These bugs are painful because they only show up at certain temperatures, voltages or trace lengths, and the logic itself looks perfect.
Even if the edge doesn't actually double-trigger, a ringback that dips into the threshold window moves the crossing time around, so you lose setup and hold margin.
And receivers don't guarantee anything between V IL and V IH , so different chips might disagree.
Data lines that are sampled after they've settled can tolerate some ringing, but clocks, resets and strobes can't.
I'd fix it at the source with termination and clean routing, and where I can't, I'd use a Schmitt-trigger input to give the receiver some hysteresis."
